resources.string: At the playhead · tap an effect to adjust it.
Returns all its controls to their defaults. Other effects are kept.
Not drawn by this version of the app.
Animate: add keyframes as you adjust controls
Zoom, mirror patterns and widescreen framing
Freeze, repeat or speed up motion
Replace or blur what is behind you
Before color looks · tap a value to reset
Adjust contrast to use the pivot.
Returns all controls to neutral and removes their keyframes. Other effects are kept.
Brightens or darkens the whole picture in stops. +1 EV doubles the light. This grades the image; it does not change the camera exposure. Highlights roll off gently.
Separates light and dark tones around the contrast pivot. 100% is unchanged. Color proportions are preserved.
Raises or lowers darker tones, while keeping the black endpoint. Use Blacks to lift or deepen the very darkest areas.
Raises or lowers brighter tones, while keeping the white endpoint. Use Whites to change the brightest areas.
Lifts or deepens the darkest endpoint. Positive values soften black; negative values deepen black with a gentle toe.
Raises or lowers the brightest endpoint. Positive values brighten whites with a gentle roll-off.
The tone that stays fixed as contrast changes. 50% is a middle display tone. Has no effect at 100% contrast.
Relative white balance: negative is cooler (blue), positive is warmer (amber). Zero preserves the recorded balance; very bright whites stay white. This is not a Kelvin setting.
Relative white balance: negative adds green, positive adds magenta. Useful for correcting a color cast.
Controls all color intensity. 100% is unchanged; 0% is black and white.
Adjusts muted colors more than already vivid ones. Positive adjustments are gentler on common skin hues.
Rotates all colors around the color wheel, preserving luminance. Zero preserves the original hues.
Blends this correction with its input. 100% applies the full correction; 0% bypasses it.
Choose a colored area. Black, white and gray have no hue to isolate.
Balance exposure, contrast, white balance and color before your look.

Start with Exposure and White balance, then adjust Contrast and Saturation. Use the tonal controls to refine shadows, midtones and highlights. Compare with Original while adjusting; clipped detail that was never recorded cannot be recovered.
Tint the picture with a single film color.
Choose a color for the whole image. Tint colors the highlights; Tone colors the shadows while keeping whites neutral. Contrast controls the separation of light and dark.
Silent cinema used tinting and toning to color whole shots and suggest mood or time of day.
Rich colors, deeper reds and dense blacks.
Use Saturation for rich color, Red depth for denser reds, and Warmth to balance the result. Lower Intensity for a gentler look and check skin tones in the preview.
Three-strip dye-transfer printing layered cyan, yellow and magenta dyes to create rich cinema color.
Muted color with strong, metallic contrast.
Strength increases contrast and removes color for a dense, metallic look. Lower it if faces or shadows lose too much detail.
Retaining silver during color-film processing produces desaturated color and dense contrast.
Turn daylight into a cool, dark night look.
Darkness and Blue make daylight footage read as night. Moonlight highlights preserve bright accents. It works best with controlled light; a bright daytime sky can still reveal the illusion.
Day-for-night photography uses exposure and color filtration to make daylight scenes read as night.
Black and white with deep shadows and contrast.
Create a monochrome image with deep shadows. Adjust Contrast and Black crush while watching darker details; add Grain or a slight shadow tint for character.
Film noir uses low-key lighting and strong shadows; colored lens filters also shaped black-and-white tones.
Bold monochrome contrast with a dark vignette.
Combine hard monochrome contrast with a dark vignette. Choose the iris shape and reduce Vignette if it hides important content near the edges.
German Expressionist cinema used stylized shadows and distorted sets, notably in The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari (1920).
Keep one color in color; make the rest monochrome.
Keep one color while the rest becomes black and white. Hue chooses the color; Hue range widens the colors retained; Softness blends their edges.
Selective color contrasts a colored detail with monochrome surroundings, as in Rumble Fish (1983).
Slide the red, green and blue images out of alignment.
Move each color layer with its X and Y sliders. Zero is the original registration; at either end a channel moves by 12% of the picture’s shorter side.
Color dye-transfer printing aligned three separate matrices to register the color image.
Flash between the original picture and its color negative.
Alternate the picture with its color negative. One cycle includes a positive and a negative image. Use the whole range or set a shorter burst.
Experimental flicker films of the 1960s intercut positive and negative images.
Mirror the picture or repeat a wedge around a movable center.

Two divisions mirror one half of the picture. Higher counts repeat a wedge around the center. Even counts alternate reflections. Odd counts repeat by rotation. The split controls move and turn the split; the source controls pan and turn the picture inside it. The picture reflects at its edges.
A camera fitted with mirrors turned ordinary workshop scenes into moving patterns in Kaleidoscope Shop (1959).
Soften bright lights with a warm glow.
Glow softens bright areas, Halation red adds warm fringes around highlights, and Flash lifts shadows. Use small amounts to retain contrast.
Film halation spreads warm light around bright highlights; diffusion and pre-exposure can soften contrast.
Film grain, softness and subtle frame movement.
Choose the grain size and amount, then add softness or gate movement. Grain animates with each frame. The frame edge option adds a rounded film gate.
Lightweight 16mm cameras helped filmmakers work outside studios and became central to documentary production.
Warm, faded home-movie color and coarse grain.
Combine faded warm color, coarse grain and an unsteady frame. Adjust Fade, Grain and Weave independently; Light leaks adds occasional warm light at the edge.
Introduced in 1965, the small-gauge cartridge format made home-movie filmmaking more accessible.
Change the frame ratio and add horizontal light flares.
Choose the frame ratio and bar style, then add horizontal highlight flares if desired. The bars remain clean above other effects.
The widescreen expansion of the 1950s brought broad compositions, anamorphic flares and distinctive lens rendering.
A quick push toward a face or detail.
A quick push toward a face or detail. Place the target with Target X and Y, adjust Zoom amount, Push duration and Hold, then choose whether to return.
Fast lens zooms became an expressive device in 1960s and 1970s westerns and martial-arts cinema.
Reduce the picture to a few colors or shades of gray.

Reduce the image to a few colors or gray levels. From scene samples the picture; Pop palettes map brightness to fixed colors. Smoothing reduces speckles. Lock palette keeps colors stable, and Re-sample captures a new palette from the current frame.
Posterization reduces continuous tones to flat bands, echoing photographic silkscreen prints of the 1960s.
Remove a green or blue screen and choose a new background.

Use a green or blue screen behind the subject. Screen color identifies the color to remove; Background replaces it with a solid color, a picture from the phone or a blurred copy of the original. Matte view shows what is kept. Despill removes colored fringes.
Color-difference travelling mattes separate a subject photographed against a blue or green backing.
Lift dark footage and clean noise. Editor only.
Brighten dark footage and reduce noise after recording, with a quick single-frame cleanup. Increase recovery gradually: strong settings can soften detail or expose color blotches.
The picture is no longer in the project.
The picture could not be added.
Palette locked to this frame · %1$d colors
The frame could not be sampled.
The preview shows a simplified version of this effect; the export draws it in full.
Taking the palette from the scene…
Insert a held frame, with optional slow push-in.

Insert a hold at the playhead. Hold duration adds time to the project; Push-in moves slowly into the still. Cut silences the sound until the footage resumes; Continue plays it on, so words can repeat when the footage resumes; Fade out over hold plays it on and fades it away.
A held frame can suspend a film at a decisive moment, as at the end of The 400 Blows (1959).
Repeat and blend frames for stuttering, smeared motion.
Repeat groups of frames for stuttering motion. Step frames sets how many frames make a group and Smear blends the motion within each group. A speed of 0.5 also slows the clip down.
Repeating printed frames produces stuttering motion, combined with blur in Chungking Express (1994).
Quick, uneven motion with a silent-film cadence.
Choose a low frame cadence for uneven motion, then adjust Speed-up, Flicker and Gate weave. Speed-up shortens the clip; Mute audio silences its sound.
Shooting fewer frames than the projection rate gives the quick, uneven movement associated with silent comedy.
No single frame to hold at the playhead
